individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper introduces Chain-of-Agents (CoA), a paradigm for training a single LLM to perform end-to-end multi-agent problem solving by dynamically activating role-playing and tool agents within one decoding process. The authors propose a multi-agent distillation framework that converts trajectories from the OAgents multi-agent system into CoA-format supervised fine-tuning data, followed by agentic reinforcement learning with DAPO. The resulting Agent Foundation Models (AFMs) are evaluated on web-agent benchmarks (MHQA, GAIA, BrowseComp, HLE, WebWalker) and code/math benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, AIME, MATH500, etc.), reporting state-of-the-art results and an 84.6% token reduction over traditional multi-agent systems. The model weights, code, and training data are open-sourced.
Strengths: Broad empirical evaluation across many web-agent and code/math benchmarks, with strong reported gains over existing TIR methods.
Practical and promising idea: distilling multi-agent collaboration trajectories into a single model reduces inference cost and enables end-to-end training.
Open-sourcing model weights, code, and training data is valuable for reproducible research and future work on agentic RL.
The RL training details, dataset composition, and efficiency analysis provide useful practical guidance.
The analysis of generalization to unseen tools, though qualitative, highlights an interesting property of the trained agent models.
Weaknesses: Potential data leakage: the RL dataset for MHQA uses the 'full set of NQ and HotpotQA' while evaluations are reported on NQ and HotpotQA; the paper does not specify whether evaluation splits were excluded from training.

No ablation isolates the contribution of the core CoA paradigm; the paper does not compare against SFT on plain ReAct trajectories from the same teacher, so it is unclear whether the benefit comes from multi-agent distillation, trajectory formatting, or simply more/better SFT data.
The name 'Chain-of-Agents' collides with prior work on long-context multi-agent collaboration (CoA), which is not cited or discussed, creating ambiguity about novelty.

Several tables are inconsistent or mislabeled: Table 12 contains duplicate AFM rows without identifying model sizes, Table 6 and Table 4 disagree on whether HotpotQA is single-hop or multi-hop, and the SFT total in Table 9 does not match the sum of its rows.

Small evaluation sets (e.g., GAIA uses 103 examples, AIME 30) are reported without confidence intervals or multiple seeds, and the efficiency analysis uses only 10 randomly sampled GAIA instances without error bars.
The generalization-to-unseen-tools analysis is qualitative and lacks quantitative metrics or systematic evaluation.
Questions: Were the evaluation splits of NQ and HotpotQA excluded from the SFT and RL datasets? Please specify exact train/test splits.
How does AFM-SFT compare to a model trained with the same data budget on plain ReAct trajectories distilled from the same teacher (OAgents) without CoA formatting and role labels?
What is the contribution of each data-filtering stage (complexity, quality, reflection enrichment, error-correction upsampling) to final performance?
In Table 12, the two AFM-SFT/AFM-RL row pairs appear to be 7B and 32B results, but the table places both under the 32B heading; please clarify which rows correspond to which model size.
How stable are the reported GAIA, AIME, and efficiency results across random seeds and evaluation samples?
Why is HotpotQA categorized as single-hop in Table 4 but listed under multi-hop in Table 6?
Limitations: No explicit contamination control for training/evaluation splits, especially for NQ and HotpotQA.
No ablations demonstrating the necessity of multi-agent distillation versus simpler trajectory synthesis.
Name overlap with prior 'Chain-of-Agents' work may cause confusion and should be differentiated.
The approach relies on external APIs (Serpapi, Jina, nsjail) which may affect reproducibility and generalization across environments.
The paper does not discuss potential societal risks or dual-use concerns of releasing powerful open-source agent models.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: This paper introduces Chain-of-Agents (CoA), a paradigm for training LLMs to solve tasks end-to-end by dynamically orchestrating multiple role-playing and tool agents within a single model. The authors propose a multi-agent distillation framework to convert trajectories from a state-of-the-art multi-agent system (OAgents) into CoA-format supervised fine-tuning data, followed by agentic reinforcement learning. The resulting Agent Foundation Models (AFMs) are evaluated on web search, code generation, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, achieving new state-of-the-art results at 7B/32B scales while using fewer tokens than conventional multi-agent systems. The code, model weights, and training data are open-sourced.
Strengths: The CoA paradigm provides a natural way to unify multi-agent collaboration and end-to-end training, extending TIR beyond single-tool ReAct loops.

The multi-agent distillation and agentic RL pipeline is a practical recipe to transfer capabilities from strong MASs into a single model, and the open-sourced resources (weights, code, data) are valuable to the community.

Extensive experiments across ~20 benchmarks show substantial gains over prior TIR methods, especially on complex web tasks (GAIA, BrowseComp, HLE) and code/math reasoning, with notable token efficiency improvements.
Weaknesses: The novelty relative to existing TIR methods is incremental: a CoA trajectory is essentially a ReAct/SFT sequence with multiple tool tags, and the training pipeline (teacher-distilled SFT + RL) resembles prior work such as Search-R1; the conceptual distinction needs sharper formalization.

The paper is difficult to reproduce because of missing implementation details (e.g., how the system prompt lists agents, how transitions between agents are decided, how OAgents trajectories are transformed into CoA format) and numerous formatting/notation errors, broken equations, and inconsistent numbers (e.g., BrowseComp 11.1 vs 11.0; duplicated references).

The evaluation claims are not always apples-to-apples: some baselines use stronger backbones or different inference strategies, and the token-efficiency analysis is based on only 10 GAIA instances without variance reporting.
The generalizability to unseen agents is only demonstrated anecdotally, and the web agent model fails on character-precise tools; there is no quantitative measure of zero-shot agent generalization.
Questions: How are the agent roles and their transition dynamics encoded in the system prompt? Is the agent set fixed at inference time, and how does the model decide to switch between Thinking/Plan/Search etc.?
What exactly does the multi-agent distillation convert from OAgents? Are the original inter-agent messages just concatenated as observations? How are role labels assigned?
The token efficiency claim (84.6% reduction) is based on only 10 GAIA samples. What is the variance, and how is 'successful task completion' normalized?
Why is OAgents the only teacher? Would distilling from other MASs (e.g., OWL, DeepResearch) improve diversity and performance?
The RL reward uses only binary correctness; for web tasks, how reliable is LLM-as-Judge across these benchmarks, and was the judge's agreement measured?
Are there any contamination checks between the SFT/RL training data and the evaluation benchmarks (especially LiveCodeBench v4/v5, GAIA, BrowseComp)?
Limitations: The approach depends heavily on a high-quality teacher MAS and a large amount of distilled data; this may not scale to environments lacking a strong teacher.
The model is only evaluated on web search and code/math tools; other tool types (e.g., visual, database) and real-world API interactions are not tested beyond one anecdote.
The filtering heuristics (e.g., 'Complexity filtering', 'Reflection enrichment') are subjective and may remove informative samples or introduce bias.
Potential environmental and economic costs of training 32B models with RL; however, the released resources mitigate this.
No discussion of failure modes, safety of code execution (sandbox noted but not evaluated), or biases in web search results.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper introduces Chain-of-Agents (CoA), a paradigm that aims to enable end-to-end multi-agent problem-solving within a single LLM by dynamically activating role-playing and tool agents. To elicit this ability, the authors propose a multi-agent distillation framework that converts successful trajectories from a state-of-the-art multi-agent system (OAgents) into CoA-style trajectories for supervised fine-tuning, followed by agentic reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks. The resulting Agent Foundation Models (AFMs) are evaluated on web agent benchmarks (GAIA, BrowseComp, HLE, multi-hop QA) and code/math benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, AIME, etc.), claiming state-of-the-art results across nearly 20 benchmarks. The paper also reports reduced inference token consumption compared to traditional multi-agent systems and open-sources models, code, and data.
Strengths: The CoA paradigm is a reasonable unification of multi-agent collaboration and end-to-end training within a single model, potentially reducing inference cost and enabling data-centric optimization.

The multi-agent distillation framework is a creative way to transfer capabilities from strong multi-agent systems (e.g., OAgents) into a single model, and the agentic RL stage extends this with verifiable rewards.
The empirical results are broad, covering web, code, and math domains, and show substantial improvements over prior TIR methods, especially at the 32B scale (e.g., 55.3% on GAIA, 59.8% on AIME25).
Open-sourcing model weights, training code, and data is a significant positive contribution to the community.
The analysis on computational efficiency (84.6% token reduction vs. OAgents) and test-time scaling demonstrates additional valuable insights.
The progressive quality filtering and RL data sampling are thoughtful attempts to ensure high-quality training data and avoid trivial samples.
Weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat limited: the CoA paradigm is essentially a role-prompting and trajectory distillation technique; the 'multi-agent' aspect appears only in the data generation source, not in the reasoning process, which is still a single-model generation. This should be better positioned against prior TIR and agent distillation works.

Crucial implementation details are missing: how are agents defined in the system prompt? How are role-playing agents (Thinking, Plan, Reflection, Verification) activated? What is the exact trajectory template (e.g., <think>...</think><tools>...</tools>)? The appendix sections for prompts are empty, making reproduction impossible.

The evaluation is not fully controlled and has inconsistencies: GAIA uses only 103 text-only examples, HLE uses 500 text-only, and some baselines are missing for certain datasets. The LLM-as-Judge (Qwen-2.5-72B) may introduce bias and is not validated against human judgments.

The 84.6% token reduction claim is based on only 10 randomly sampled GAIA instances, which is not statistically robust, and the variance and performance parity with OAgents on those samples are not reported.
The quality filtering uses arbitrary thresholds (e.g., <5 interactions, r_q<=0.3) and heuristics without clear justification or sensitivity analysis.
The web-agent RL reward is a binary LLM-as-Judge score without any format reward or anti-hacking constraints, which could lead to reward hacking; the paper does not analyze this risk.

The paper contains numerous typos, malformed equations (e.g., Equation 7 has broken LaTeX), and poorly formatted tables (e.g., Table 6 column misalignment, Table 12 duplicate rows for AFM-SFT/AFM-RL without clear model size labels), which significantly hurt readability and credibility.

The generalization analysis (Section 5.2) is anecdotal, relying on a single case study, and does not provide quantitative results or statistical evidence for the claim that code agents generalize better to unseen tools.

The paper does not disclose several limitations, such as potential contamination from using benchmark-derived training data (e.g., NQ, HotpotQA, LiveCodeBench v1-v3) and the dependency on the teacher multi-agent system's capability ceiling.
Questions: How are the role-playing agents (Thinking, Plan, Reflection, Verification) and tool agents (Search, Crawl, Code) precisely instantiated in the model's prompt? Are they just special tokens, and how is the activation decision made at inference time?

What is the exact trajectory format used in SFT? The paper mentions <think>, <tools>, <observation>, <reflection>, and <answer> tags, but the full template and how observations are masked are not specified.
How sensitive are the results to the choice of LLM-as-Judge (Qwen-2.5-72B)? Was the judge validated against human labels or other judges, and what is the inter-judge agreement?

In Table 12, AFM-SFT and AFM-RL rows appear twice, with different numbers. Could the authors clarify the correct results for 7B and 32B? Also, why does AFM-7B outperform ReTool-32B on LiveCodeBench v5?
What is the exact composition of the RL dataset for web agents (e.g., number of samples per source)? The paper mentions 169,615 for MHQA and 10,427 for Web Agent, but the source breakdown is unclear.
For the efficiency claim, what is the performance of AFM on the 10 GAIA instances compared to OAgents and WebThinker? Is the 84.6% token reduction with or without performance normalization?

How are the agent activation sequences chosen? Is the model trained with free-form generation, or is there any constrained decoding or grammars? What happens if the model produces an invalid tool call?
The paper claims 'native end-to-end multi-agent problem-solving.' Does the model explicitly learn a policy over agent identities, or is the agent role just a prefix in the generated text?
What is the computational cost of the multi-agent distillation process and RL training? The paper only reports inference cost reductions, not training costs.
Limitations: The evaluation is limited to English, text-only tasks; the paper does not address multimodal or real-world interactive environments, which are critical for general agent deployment.
The student model's performance is bounded by the teacher multi-agent system (OAgents); this ceiling is not discussed or analyzed.
The LLM-as-Judge reward may cause the model to overfit to judge preferences rather than true answer correctness, and the paper does not investigate this.
Training data includes benchmark-derived sets (e.g., NQ, HotpotQA, LiveCodeBench v1-v3) that overlap with evaluation, raising contamination concerns despite the filtering attempts.
The paper does not analyze the stability or failure modes of the CoA paradigm, such as what happens when the model repeatedly chooses the same agent or enters a loop.
The efficiency analysis is based on a small sample and does not account for the overhead of the teacher multi-agent system used to generate trajectories.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper introduces Chain-of-Agents (CoA), a paradigm for training large language models to perform multi-agent-style problem solving end-to-end within a single model, using dynamically activated role-playing and tool agents. To train such models (called Agent Foundation Models, AFMs), the authors propose multi-agent distillation from an existing multi-agent system (OAgents) together with agentic reinforcement learning. Experiments across web search, multi-hop QA, code generation, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that AFM achieves state-of-the-art results with reduced token consumption compared to traditional multi-agent systems.
Strengths: Proposes a novel training paradigm that unifies multi-agent collaboration and end-to-end learning in a single model, addressing efficiency and data-centric learning limitations of traditional MAS.
Multi-agent distillation from OAgents is an interesting and practical way to convert MAS trajectories into CoA SFT data, and the filtering/reflection enrichment is thoughtful.
Extensive empirical evaluation across many benchmarks (7 MHQA, GAIA, BrowseComp, HLE, WebWalker, LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, AIME, etc.) with strong results, especially at 32B scale.
Analysis of token efficiency showing 84.6% reduction vs MAS and generalization to unseen agents is valuable.
Open-sourcing models, code, and data is a significant contribution to the community.
Weaknesses: Writing quality is poor: typos, broken equations, inconsistent table formats (e.g., Table 6 and Table 12 have formatting issues), duplicated references, and incomplete appendix prompts hurt clarity and reproducibility.

The novelty of 'Chain-of-Agents' over existing TIR is somewhat limited—it is a tool-integrated reasoning with multiple role-playing tags; the paper does not provide a rigorous formalization or clear advantages in terms of capabilities beyond what a sufficiently expressive TIR model could do.
The claim of distilling 'any state-of-the-art multi-agent frameworks' is overclaimed because only OAgents is used as teacher; generality is not demonstrated.

Comparisons are not always fair: some strong baselines use stronger backbones (e.g., QwQ-32B vs Qwen2.5-32B), and the paper sometimes claims SOTA while not beating baselines on individual datasets (e.g., NQ, HotpotQA in single-hop).

Evaluation lacks ablations: no controlled experiments isolating contributions of multi-agent distillation vs simple SFT on the same data, reflection enrichment, error-correction upsampling, or the proposed RL reward design.

Limited discussion of limitations and potential negative societal impacts (e.g., web agents may retrieve unreliable information, autonomous code execution risks).

Did the authors consider ablating the multi-agent distillation from OAgents vs directly using OAgents' outputs as flat ReAct trajectories? Does the specific role tag structure matter?
How is the LLM-as-Judge reward calibrated for open-ended web tasks? What are the inter-judge agreement rates?
The paper reports 84.6% token reduction vs traditional MAS; how was this measured exactly across all frameworks, and what is the variance over more samples?
What is the contamination risk for benchmarks like LiveCodeBench v4-v5 and AIME25 given the training data includes similar sources? How did authors handle contamination?
Why is AFM not consistently better on single-hop QA datasets like NQ compared to Search-R1/ZeroSearch? Does the CoA paradigm trade off efficiency for single-hop tasks?
Limitations: Reliance on a single teacher (OAgents) limits diversity of distilled collaboration patterns.

The CoA paradigm still requires manually defining agent roles and tools in the system prompt; generalization to truly novel tools is limited, as shown in Section 5.2 (web agent fails on format-constrained tools).
LLM-as-judge for web agent rewards may introduce bias and is not verifiable.
Training data contamination with benchmark distributions not thoroughly analyzed.
Scalability of training with many tool calls and long contexts may be expensive.
Potential negative societal impacts of autonomous web agents (e.g., misinformation, privacy) not discussed.

review.Summary: The paper introduces Chain-of-Agents (CoA), a paradigm in which a single LLM performs multi-agent-style problem solving end-to-end by dynamically activating role-playing and tool agents within one decoding process. To train models for this paradigm, the authors propose multi-agent distillation: they record trajectories from an existing multi-agent system (OAgents), filter and reformat them into CoA-style traces for supervised fine-tuning, and then apply agentic reinforcement learning with outcome rewards. The resulting models, called Agent Foundation Models (AFMs), are evaluated on multi-hop QA, web-agent benchmarks (GAIA, BrowseComp, HLE, WebWalker), code generation, and mathematical reasoning. The authors report state-of-the-art results across many benchmarks and an 84.6% reduction in token consumption relative to multi-agent systems, and they state that all weights, code, and data are open-sourced.
Strengths: The CoA paradigm is a sensible and practical synthesis of multi-agent collaboration and end-to-end trainable tool-integrated reasoning, addressing a real inefficiency of conventional multi-agent frameworks.
The multi-agent distillation pipeline is a concrete, transferable recipe for converting multi-agent system trajectories into SFT data, and the four-stage filtering adds useful quality control.
Extensive empirical evaluation across many tasks and model scales (7B/32B) shows broad improvements over several TIR baselines, especially on GAIA, AIME25, LiveCodeBench, and CodeContests.
The observed token-efficiency advantage over a traditional multi-agent system, even if preliminary, is an important benefit for practical deployment.
Releasing model weights, training code, and data is valuable for reproducibility and future research on agentic RL.
The generalization analysis on unseen tools, while anecdotal, is an interesting and relevant probe of whether CoA training transfers across agent types.
Weaknesses: The manuscript is clearly incomplete: several figures are placeholders ([REDACTED]), Table 8 is a figure placeholder, many references are redacted, and the Appendix prompts are empty; this prevents reproduction and makes the submission not self-contained.

Numerous inconsistencies and errors in tables undermine confidence: e.g., Table 6 contains implausible baseline values (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on TriviaQA=35.6 but 1.2 in another column with wrong average), Table 12 has two unlabelled AFM-SFT rows with very different numbers, and Table 7 mixes model sizes unsystematically.

No direct same-backbone comparison is made against multi-agent systems such as OAgents or OWL using Qwen2.5-32B; the comparisons against GPT-4.1-based frameworks are confounded by different base models and prompt engineering.
The computational efficiency claim is based on only 10 randomly sampled GAIA instances and lacks controlled conditions, variance estimates, or a breakdown of where token savings come from.

The web-agent reward relies on an LLM-as-Judge (Qwen-2.5-72B) without any validation of judge accuracy, calibration, or correlation with human judgments; this is a potential source of reward hacking and biased results.

There is likely undesirable overlap between SFT and RL data: the MHQA RL set uses the full NQ/HotpotQA while SFT samples from the same sources, and the code-agent SFT/RL sets are intentionally not deduplicated; this can inflate results and masks true generalization.

The test-time scaling analysis is limited to Pass@3 and Best-of-3 with an external judge, which triples inference cost and is not compared under equal compute budgets; calling this 'agentic test-time scaling' is misleading.
Claims that CoA 'supports any multi-agent system' are not substantiated; in practice only OAgents is distilled and a fixed, small set of agents is used.
No statistical significance tests or error bars are reported for the many small test sets (e.g., AIME has 30 problems, GAIA has 103), where performance differences of a few points are not meaningful.
The paper lacks a discussion of limitations and negative societal impacts, and does not address potential safety concerns of open-sourced autonomous web/code agents.
Questions: What exactly is the token-level interface for activating and switching agents in CoA? Is it just a set of special tags (<think>, <tools>, <reflection>) or are there dedicated role tokens, and how is the model constrained to emit valid agent transitions?

How do the CoA trajectories differ from standard ReAct trajectories beyond the use of role labels and reflection blocks? Could a simpler ReAct-style format with richer prompts achieve the same results?
Why is there no direct comparison with OAgents or OWL running on the same Qwen-2.5-32B backbone? This would isolate the benefit of CoA from backbone/model differences.

In the efficiency analysis, were the MAS and TIR baselines run under identical tool-calling budgets and hardware? What is the variance in token counts and success rates across the 10 sampled GAIA instances?
For the web-agent reward, was the LLM-as-Judge validated against human labels or known ground truth? What is the judge's false-positive/false-negative rate on each benchmark?
The MHQA RL set uses the full NQ and HotpotQA while SFT was trained on a filtered subset of the same datasets. What is the overlap, and how do results change if the RL set is disjoint from SFT?
In Table 12, two rows are labeled AFM-SFT with different values; are these 7B and 32B respectively? If so, please label them clearly and correct the table.
For AFM-Pass@3 and AFM-Bo3, how is the final answer selected? Is an external judge used in both cases, and how does this compare to simple majority voting without a judge?
How does the model decide when to invoke a reflection or verification agent? Are these decisions learned entirely from distilled trajectories, or are they partially rule-based?
The generalization experiment on unseen tools uses only two case studies. Can you provide aggregate success rates and a more systematic evaluation of zero-shot agent generalization?
Limitations: The paper is not reproducible in its current form because key figures, tables, and appendix prompts are missing or redacted.
The multi-agent distillation is only demonstrated with one teacher system (OAgents) and a fixed set of agents, so the claimed generality to arbitrary multi-agent systems is unproven.
The efficiency measurement is under-powered (10 samples) and lacks statistical rigor.
The RL reward for web tasks uses an unvalidated LLM judge, which may introduce bias and reward hacking.
Test-time scaling results confound compute (3x rollouts) with method improvements and rely on an external judge for answer selection.
Potential data contamination due to SFT/RL overlap is not addressed.
No safety or societal-impact analysis is provided for the open-sourced autonomous web and code agents.

review.Summary: The paper proposes Chain-of-Agents (CoA), a training paradigm that enables a single LLM to solve tasks end-to-end by dynamically activating role-playing and tool agents during decoding. The authors curate CoA-style SFT data from OAgents multi-agent system trajectories, followed by agentic reinforcement learning, yielding Agent Foundation Models evaluated on web, code, and math benchmarks. They report SOTA results and an 84.6% token reduction, and open-source models, data, and code.
Strengths: The CoA paradigm offers a practical synthesis of multi-agent collaboration and end-to-end tool-integrated reasoning, with potential inference cost savings compared to explicit multi-agent systems.
Multi-agent distillation from OAgents with quality filtering and reflection enrichment is a concrete, transferable recipe, and releasing weights/code/data is valuable.
Extensive evaluation across many benchmarks shows substantial gains over several TIR baselines, especially at 32B scale on GAIA, AIME25, LiveCodeBench, and CodeContests.
The token-efficiency analysis, while preliminary, highlights an important practical advantage; and the generalization probe to unseen tools is an interesting question.
Open-sourcing resources facilitates reproducibility and future research.
Weaknesses: The manuscript is incomplete and lacks clarity: missing figures, empty appendix prompts, broken equations, malformed tables (e.g., duplicate/unlabelled AFM rows, inconsistent baseline values), and redacted references make reproduction impossible.

Potential data leakage/contamination is not adequately handled; MHQA RL uses the full NQ/HotpotQA while evaluation uses the same sets, and code-agent SFT/RL are not deduplicated; this can inflate results.

No ablations isolate the contribution of multi-agent distillation vs. simpler ReAct SFT, nor of the filtering/reflection stages or the RL reward design; no same-backbone comparison against teacher MASs such as OAgents/OWL.

Novelty is limited/incremental: CoA is essentially ReAct with multiple role tags and teacher-distillation; the name collides with prior 'Chain-of-Agents' work and the conceptual distinction from existing TIR is not rigorously formalized.
Efficiency claims rely on 10 GAIA samples without variance or controlled conditions; LLM-as-Judge rewards are unvalidated and may induce reward hacking/bias.
Evaluation has small test sets without confidence intervals, unfair baseline configurations, inconsistent SOTA claims, and anecdotal-only evidence for generalization.
Safety/societal risks of open-sourced autonomous agents are not discussed.
Questions: Were NQ/HotpotQA evaluation splits excluded from SFT/RL training, and what is the exact overlap?
How does AFM compare to a model trained on plain ReAct trajectories from OAgents under the same data budget?
What is the exact mechanism for selecting/activating agents, and can the model emit invalid transitions?
Is the LLM-as-Judge reward validated against human labels, and what is the inter-judge agreement?
Why are there duplicate/unlabelled AFM rows in Table 12, and what are the correct 7B/32B results?
What is the variance of the 84.6% token reduction claim over more samples?
What evidence shows that CoA supports any multi-agent system beyond OAgents?
Limitations: Dependency on one teacher (OAgents) and fixed agent set limits demonstrated generality.
Reliance on external APIs (Serpapi, Jina, nsjail) affects reproducibility and generalization.
Potential contamination and lack of deduplication between training/evaluation data.
Unvalidated LLM-as-Judge for web rewards and small efficiency sample.
No analysis of failure modes, reward hacking, loops, or safety of autonomous execution.
Limited to English text-only tasks and a small set of tools.
